summary: Specifies an experimental ICMPv6 message type for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). The message dynamically updates identifier and locator bindings for an existing ILNP session. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: ILNP separates a node's name from the addresses that reach it, so a node can have several addresses at once and change them without disturbing its conversations. RFC 6743 defines the message a node sends when its addresses change. The message lists every address that is currently valid, each with a preference and a time limit, and every correspondent replies to say it arrived.

how does ilnpv6 handle node mobility
what icmp type is used for locator updates
subtitle: A message that lets a moving IPv6 node tell its correspondents about its new locations.

tldr.problem: In ILNP, a node's locator can change when it moves or gains a new network connection, but its correspondents need to know about the change to keep sending packets to the right place.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an ICMPv6 message type, 156, that carries the node's full set of valid locators with a preference and a lifetime for each. A node sends it to every correspondent of every active unicast session when its set changes.
tldr.outcome: ILNPv6 nodes can keep their correspondents up to date without tearing the session down. The document is Experimental and comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

today: RFC 6743 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is one of the ILNP documents from the IRTF Routing Research Group, sitting alongside the architecture in RFC 6740, the engineering considerations in RFC 6741 and the IPv4 counterpart in RFC 6745. The document itself notes that its views were considered controversial, and that ILNP is a research direction rather than a deployed protocol.

sections.title: Why ILNP Needs a Locator Update
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol is an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It separates a node's identifier, which is stable, from its locators, which are the addresses that reach it. A node may have several locators at once, and the set changes when the node moves, when it gains or loses a network connection, or when it multihomes.

The document is part of the ILNP set, which had extensive review in the IRTF Routing Research Group, and the authors note that the views in it were considered controversial but that the group reached a consensus that it should still be published. It places ILNP among the approaches being explored to evolve the Internet architecture, alongside the Identifier/Locator Split class of proposals, in a period when scalability of inter-domain routing, site and node multihoming and node mobility were all active concerns.

ILNP has more than one possible engineering instantiation. ILNPv6 is the instance based on and backwards compatible with IPv6, and ILNPv4 the one based on IPv4. This document defines the new ICMPv6 Locator Update message, used by an ILNP node to inform its correspondent nodes of any change to its set of valid locators. It must only be used for ILNPv6 sessions, and authentication is always required.
sections.plainLanguage: ILNP gives a node a stable name and separate addresses that reach it. When those addresses change, the node has to tell the machines it is talking to, and this message is how it does that.

sections.title: Where This Fits in the ILNP Set
sections.content:
The memo points at the other documents in the set for everything it does not cover. RFC 6740 is the main architectural description of ILNP, including the concept of operations. RFC 6741 covers the engineering and implementation considerations common to both ILNPv4 and ILNPv6, and RFC 6742 defines additional DNS resource records that support ILNP.

Two documents matter most for this message. RFC 6744 defines an IPv6 Nonce Destination Option used by ILNPv6 nodes to signal that they are operating in ILNP mode and to prevent off-path attacks against ILNP ICMP messages; the nonce is used with all ILNPv6 ICMPv6 Locator Update messages exchanged between correspondents. RFC 6745 defines the matching message for IPv4, and RFC 6746 defines the IPv4 options that carry the nonce and the identifier for ILNPv4. RFC 6747 covers extensions to the Address Resolution Protocol for ILNPv4, and RFC 6748 describes optional deployment functions that are not needed to operate ILNP.
sections.plainLanguage: This message is one piece of a larger set. The architecture, the shared engineering rules and the DNS records live in their own documents, and the nonce option that protects this message is defined separately.

sections.title: The ICMPv6 Locator Update Message
sections.content:
The message has ICMP type 156 and code 0, and the checksum is calculated in the same way as for any other ICMPv6 message. The number of locators field gives how many 64-bit locator values are advertised and must not be zero. Each locator is followed by a 16-bit preference, which says how preferable it is relative to the other valid locators and uses the same syntax and meaning as the preference values for L64 records in RFC 6742, and a lifetime, which is the maximum number of seconds that particular locator may be considered valid, normally the same as the DNS lifetime of the corresponding L64 record.

The operation field says whether the message is a Locator Update Advertisement, with value 0x01, or a Locator Update Acknowledgement, with value 0x02. All other values are reserved. The reserved field must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and might be used for some protocol function in future.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a short header followed by one block per address: the address itself, a number saying how much the sender prefers it, and how long it stays valid.

sections.title: Sending, Acknowledging and Storing the Update
sections.content:
A node whose set of valid locators has changed must send a Locator Update Advertisement to each correspondent node for each active unicast ILNP session. The receiver of a valid advertisement, meaning the authentication checks all passed and the advertisement came from a current correspondent, must send a Locator Update Acknowledgement back. The acknowledgement body is identical to the advertisement body except for the operation value.

A node sending an update must include all currently valid locator values in the message, and a node receiving a valid update must replace the previously current set of locators for that correspondent in its own Identifier Locator Communication Cache with the newly received set. Every implementation needs to cope with a large number of locators in a single message, because a multihomed node or site might have many upstream links to different service providers, each with its own locator value.

To keep the incremental deployability and backwards compatibility that ILNP needs, the network layer needs a mode bit in the Transport Control Block, or its equivalent, to track which IP sessions use the classic IPv6 mode and which use the Identifier/Locator Split mode. The message has no impact on any transport protocol: it may affect where packets for a given transport-layer session are sent, but decoupling transport protocols and transport-layer session information from network-layer changes is an ILNP design objective.
sections.plainLanguage: The advertisement lists every address that currently works, not just the ones that changed, and the receiver replaces its whole list for that correspondent with what it receives. The receiver then says it has arrived, so the sender knows the change has landed.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
The message uses the same checksum calculation as any other ICMPv6 message, so a node that does not know the type can still check it and discard it.

When ILNPv6 is not in use, the receiving IPv6 mode must discard the ICMP Locator Update packet without processing it. The memo calls this standard behaviour for a non-ILNPv6 node when it receives an ICMPv6 message with an unknown header field value. That is what lets the protocol be deployed one node at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer that does not use this protocol simply throws the message away, so the message can be introduced gradually.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the overall ILNP architecture are in RFC 6740 and the common ones in RFC 6741. The message must only be used for ILNPv6 sessions.

The ILNP Nonce Destination Option from RFC 6744 must be present in packets carrying the message, and the received nonce must hold the correct value for the packet to be accepted and passed on for processing. If either requirement is not met, the packet must be discarded as a forgery and a security event should be logged. Sessions in higher risk environments should use IP Security for ILNP in addition to the nonce option; using IPsec does not permit the packet to be sent without the nonce option, because the nonce lets a receiver do an inexpensive check before any costly cryptographic calculation.

Two further points are made. Implementations must cope with a message containing a large number of locator and preference values without developing a security fault such as a stack overflow. And if the nonce value is predictable, an off-path attacker might be able to forge data or control packets, a risk that is also mitigated by the common practice of IP source address filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: The message must carry a nonce that only the real sender could know, and a receiver that finds it wrong throws the packet away and logs it. The nonce is cheap to check, so it is checked before any expensive cryptography is done.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 156, the ICMPv6 type assigned for this message.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: The ICMPv6 checksum, calculated as for any other ICMPv6 message.

fields.name: Num of Locs
fields.desc: How many locators are advertised. This field must not be zero.

fields.name: Operation
fields.desc: 0x01 for an advertisement, 0x02 for an acknowledgement.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Locator
fields.desc: A 64-bit locator currently valid for the sending node. The block is repeated once per locator.

fields.name: Preference
fields.desc: How preferable this locator is relative to the others, as for L64 records.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: The maximum number of seconds this locator may be considered valid.

items.label: Locator Update Advertisement
items.desc: Sent by a node whose set of valid locators has changed.

items.label: Locator Update Acknowledgement
items.desc: Sent back by the receiver of a valid advertisement.

messages.label: Locator Update Advertisement
messages.note: The full set of currently valid locators, with a preference and lifetime for each.

messages.label: Locator Update Acknowledgement
messages.note: The same body, with the operation value changed.
